rationale: B wins because it is more useful under pressure: it keeps asking the questions a real editor will ask before letting the founder run around with a shiny number. Its line, "Is $342,000 a mean or a median," is exactly the kind of methodological tripwire that saves a pitch from embarrassment. A is strong, but "Ramp Turns Its $80 Billion Payments Network Into a Procurement Intelligence Engine" slides toward founder-deck moat talk before the facts have earned it.
gaps_in_A: "200 real customers" overstates the supplied fact. The update says a 200-company beta, not that all 200 were customers or referenceable customers.
"first public signal of Ramp explicitly turning payment data into procurement intelligence" is not in the update. That could be true, but this set treats it as known.
"an advantage a standalone spend-management tool sourcing data from integrations or uploads doesn't have" invents competitor context. Good strategic instinct, bad evidentiary hygiene.
The next step jumps to "journalist-fit-check" before resolving the biggest blocker: whether the $342,000 is identified savings or realized savings.
gaps_in_B: "charging for the workflow" and "the paid layer coming later this year" go past the facts. The update says enterprise tier, not price or monetization model.
"a bot reading the fine print" implies contract-term analysis. The supplied facts say the agent scans spend and drafts emails, not that it reads contracts.
"a meaningful share of SaaS revenue is renewal inertia" is a plausible market argument, but it is not supported by the update and needs an analyst or vendor-side source.
"beta has the receipts" is punchy, but it risks overstating proof if Ramp only identified savings rather than verified realized savings.
